1	# Rewriting a skill
2	
3	The skills are written for a reader new to the repository, which every agent is. A skill is a minimal set: it holds only the change to what the model does by itself, and leans on what its training already does well. Each rule states a goal or a principle, with the benefit that it brings, and the reader applies it with judgement. A rule is not a program of steps and conditions. A principle with its reason reaches the cases that it does not name. Many instructions, each for its own case, conflict, and the reader must then settle which one holds.
4	
5	**writer**
6	: Headless session that makes every edit of the project skills, started and resumed by `explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, with its standing brief `explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md`.
7	
8	**cold read**
9	: Reading of a rewritten part by a worker given only the skill (`explorations/coordinator/skill-cold-read-brief.md`). It flags each passage that would send it wrong or make it search, with its confidence, and each undefined term.
10	
11	## The method
12	
13	1. Draft the outline first, with a home for every rule that moves.
14	2. Have the writer write each part whole, by the seven principles of `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`. A rewrite is never longer than the text that it replaces.
15	3. Run a cold read. Review its flags, and have the writer fix them. Only then have a worker put a change that waits for the curator's yes on the page of skill drafts (step 4).
16	4. Land the change after its cold read, unless it waits for the curator's yes (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"). Put a change that waits under "Proposed changes" on the page of skill drafts: one item for each section that it rewrites, a whole part included, each with its new text whole, in the form of `SKILL.md`, "Pages".
17	5. Brief each comment of the curator to the writer, rather than rewrite it yourself. A comment marks a problem area: the writer fixes its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
18	6. Settle the writer's minor decisions from the record. `SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions", says which changes wait for the curator, and how a new rule is named.
19	7. After each change to the coordinator skill or to `fortress-repo` lands, have a worker update that skill's page: the page of skill drafts for the coordinator skill, the page of `fortress-repo` changes for `fortress-repo`. The boot note holds both links. Give the worker the page's URL, and have it publish by that URL. The record-landing workflow runs this update itself for the changes to `fortress-repo` that follow a landing (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). The page of skill drafts has two sections, and the page of `fortress-repo` changes has only the first:
20	   - Landed changes: only the landed changes that the curator has not read, so that no change lands unseen while the curator is away. The items stand oldest first, numbered on from the page's last item, so every item that the curator finds there is new:
21	     - If the curator says, on the page or in chat, that they have read the page up to an item, the next update removes that item and every older item. Before each update, the worker reads every comment thread on the page, sent to Claude or not. A comment on a landed item that only says that the curator read it, such as "LGTM", is such a word, at the comment's time; write the newest such word and its time in the boot note's "Pages" line of that page. Every other comment, a yes on a draft among them, drops no item, and the worker quotes it to you. The page worker and the record-landing workflow's page stage both read it there. You may have the update made at once, without waiting for the next landing.
22	     - A draft is an item under "Proposed changes" that waits for the curator's yes. Its landing, the commit of the approved words, gets no item, unless it fixed a hit of the skills' lint, `explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py`, or a wrong path or section name: then one item shows the fix alone. The skill writer first runs the lint and checks the draft's paths and section names; the fix needs no second cold read. Any other change is a change of its own and goes the way its kind goes.
23	     - Every other item stays until the curator says, on the page or in chat, that they have read it.
24	     - A folded item is an item into which a later change was folded (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). It strikes through the text before its first change, marks every word added since, and lists each change's reason in order.
25	     - The curator's word that they read the page up to an item drops a folded item only if the fold was published before the word's time. Otherwise the item stays, with the fold marked.
26	     - If a change touches the passages of two items that the curator has not said they read, fold it into each. Its part outside them gets its own item.
27	     - The one item that a draft's landing fix gets is folded too, if its passage has an item that the curator has not said they read.
28	
29	     The item takes the form of a landed item in `SKILL.md`, "Pages". It shows the change against the skill's text before it, or, for an approved draft whose words changed at the landing, against the approved words. It gives the change's reason, which may come from a cold read, a hit of the skills' lint, a fix at a draft's landing, or the record entry that the orientation workflow, in update mode, took in. The reason says in plain words what was wrong and what the text now says. It never cites a cold read's flag by its code or number, a judge's ruling by its number, or an item of a task by its number.
30	   - Proposed changes: the items that wait for the curator's yes. When an approved item lands, a worker takes it off this section.
31	
32	- Run `skill-writer.sh new <task-file>` for a fresh writer, and `skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>` for its next task, within the hour. Start a fresh writer after a pass over a whole skill, or after your compaction.
33	- The writer edits and commits the skill files. You push, except inside the record-landing workflow, which pushes the writer's commits itself.
34	- If a part that the curator approved is written again, have a Fable reviewer compare the two. Where it finds a regression, it writes a synthesis of both, never a wholesale revert.
35	- After a rule enters a skill from the curator's words, check that the skill caught the meaning, by a cold read or a test.
36	- If a practice that a skill states is in question, have a Sonnet scout check what the workers actually did. If they found a better way, write that way into the skill.
37	- Keep batch structure out of `fortress-repo`. The workflow or the brief sets which roles exist, and who builds, checks, commits and pushes.
38	- After each landing, the orientation workflow updates `fortress-repo`'s `references/revival-changes.md` (`references/batch.md`, "The landing", step 4). `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` keeps only what does not change from batch to batch.

40	## The coordinator skill
41	
42	This skill is rewritten by a heavier method, since the roles that it holds must not be lost:
43	
44	- In the list of kept rules that goes into the writer's task (below), put how to talk to the curator in each situation, as a principle.
45	- Organize the record as the model organizes knowledge by itself, never against it. This is the rewrite's highest risk.
46	- Name the session's modes first: here, the six parts.
47	- Run the baseline interview (`explorations/coordinator/baseline-interview/README.md`) for each new model of this session. Keep only what the model would not do by itself.
48	- Keep a rule if the failure that it guards against is on record. The interview alone drops nothing.
49	- Write the list of kept rules into the writer's task. The writer writes from scratch, without reading the old skill. A worker then checks the draft against that list, and the cold read follows.
50	- Have every cold reader of this skill read it as the coordinating session, which uses it, not as a worker new to the repository.

1	# Planning the road
2	
3	`explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md` holds the phases, the questions for the curator in the order they are needed, and the parked items. Keep every open question there, in the order it needs deciding, and none only in your context.
4	
5	**nine steps**
6	: Order in which a fork is answered from the evidence: (1) what the mathematics says; (2) what each path does today, measured; (3) what the specification says under every spelling; (4) what the library does in the same family; (5) where the designers departed from Java; (6) what peer languages and their implementations do; (7) what the commits say; (8) the derivation from the curator's principles in POSITIONS; (9) the decision, yours or the curator's (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"). Steps 3, 5 and 7 give the team's word, step 4 the library, and step 6 the peers; the order sets no precedence. `SKILL.md` gives the peers their place.
7	
8	**re-approval rows**
9	: Earlier decisions put to the curator again, parked in PLAN, "Off the path, parked".
10	
11	## Procedures
12	
13	- Ask for the curator's answers in PLAN's order, after you check each question against the three principles. Raise the re-approval rows and other parked items only when the work reaches them.
14	- If a probe can answer a known fork, run it while you plan, before the batch is briefed, so that the worker gets a task with the decision made. If the fork is consequential, put the probe's result to the curator as an ask.
15	- Answer each fork by the nine steps. Seek one global rule from type theory, and from the peers' implementations where the peers weigh (`SKILL.md`, "The curator's role and decisions"), not a rule on a rule.
16	- Put re-approval rows to the curator one theme per message, each row in detail, with the ask's short primer (`SKILL.md`, "An ask", item 2) and what makes sense in a high-performance language. The count of reversals is not the measure.
17	- Give idle time to the parked research in PLAN. It needs no go, but a new deliverable does: discuss it with the curator before you make it.
18	- Park what needs the curator's machine; do not simulate it.

1	# Keeping the record
2	
3	How workers read the record, and edit it when a brief asks, is `fortress-repo`'s records part.
4	
5	**history**
6	: `FACTS-history.md` or `POSITIONS-history.md`. Under each number, one block per change: a provenance line (the time, the kind of change, the report section, the commit, who, why) and the line as it stood before.
7	
8	**pointer**
9	: Another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, with a few words on its subject: "It builds P-48, on a type parameter that a call does not fix."
10	
11	**pass**
12	: Your rewrite of what a worker wrote into entries of the form below.
13	
14	## What an entry is
15	
16	An entry reads on its own. A reader who knows the language, or can look it up in the `fortress-repo` skill, can tell what it says without the conversation or the batch behind it. The entry lets a worker or you act right without opening the report, and says when the report is needed. Its number is permanent and never reused. Its title and text are rewritten freely, since the number is the key.
17	
18	- A FACTS entry holds, after its number and a bold title that states the fact: what is established now, and under which conditions; what it means for the work, such as what it blocks or which row or decision it bears on; its evidence: the test that gates it, or its source, and whether it was observed, read in the code or inferred; the decision it builds, by number and subject; and the report section that holds the detail.
19	- A POSITIONS entry holds, after its number and a bold title: what the curator decided about the project, and why, in one or two sentences; where it applies; and what it requires of the work. It may point to a fact that it rests on, in the sentence that needs it. `P-48+` finds every fact that points to it.
20	- A POSITIONS entry states the curator's meaning in the record's register, and every fact in it is correct. It is the smallest text from which a fresh worker or coordinator, with the skills loaded, decides right. Workers and you decide by it where the curator is not asked, so a wrong premise in it spreads to each of those decisions.
21	- Give as an entry's reason the ground of its own case, such as the specification's text, the library's code or a measurement. Never give a rule that holds for every decision, such as the team's later word (P-26).
22	- POSITIONS holds only the curator's decisions. A choice that a worker made and landed without the curator's word is a fact about the tree. Its FACTS entry says that a worker chose it, and its review-queue item names that entry.
23	- An entry states the present, or what holds for all time. It holds no plan and no status: no state words such as "Built." or "Still to build:", no PLAN phase or item, no review-queue item, and no words that it waits for the curator's review. PLAN and the review queue name the entries that their items concern.
24	- If the tree does not yet do what a decision or the team's design asks, the missing part is a row of the gap ledger. The entry may name it as "row N", with a few words on what the row holds. In an entry, "row N" always names a row of the gap ledger.
25	- A pointer that stays in an entry carries a few words on what it holds, such as a ledger row's subject. A bare list of numbers goes to the history.
26	- A handle that only made sense in a past conversation, such as "answer 9", goes to the history.
27	- Quote the curator only where the exact words are the decision. Otherwise condense the words into the position, keeping the part of the rule that cuts. Check the condensed text against the words before you write it. The dictated words go to the history, with their time.
28	- A count that each landing changes has one entry with its current value, what it counts, the kinds with the largest share, and how to read a move. Other entries give its number. A count from one measurement says so.
29	- An entry holds one claim that can be kept up to date on its own, with its conditions, exceptions and evidence. Split an entry when its claims answer different questions and change apart. Before you split, look for an entry that already holds the claim, and move the text there. After a split, grep the record for the old number, and repoint each pointer that meant the claim that moved.
30	- If several entries together establish a conclusion that workers keep working out again, make it a sentence of the entry that owns its subject, with pointers to the entries it rests on. The pass updates it when one of them changes. Add a new entry only if no entry owns it. Leave a conclusion nobody has checked in its report, out of the entries.
31	- Keep an entry near 600 characters. This is a check, not a cap, and no reason to split: an entry may pass it if a question below keeps a sentence.
32	- Write halfway to ASD-STE100.
33	
34	Ask of each sentence, and act on the answer:
35	
36	1. Would the reader do otherwise without it? Keep it.
37	2. Would the reader misread another sentence without it? Keep it.
38	3. Does it tell how the fact came about: a date, a batch, a correction? Move it to the history.
39	4. Is it detail needed only while doing the work: a line number, a list of sites, a timing? Leave it in the report, and name the section.
40	5. Does another entry or a skill say it? Give that entry's number, or the skill's part.
41	6. Can a reader new to the project follow every word? Name the kind of each count.
42	
43	In a consolidation of FACTS, judge each entry by six checks. Mark each one pass, fail, or unresolved where evidence is still needed, and quote the passage that fails:
44	
45	- Scope: the title and the text agree on the path, the conditions and the limits, and claim no more than the evidence shows.
46	- Present meaning: a reader can tell the current property, or a measurement bounded to its day, without rebuilding a batch's work.
47	- Evidence: the cited support exists and holds the claim, and the entry states the kind of its evidence and its uncertainty.
48	- Comprehension: a reader can restate the fact and what it means. Subjects, referents and terms are plain.
49	- Ownership: the entry has one subject. No repair history or copied count hides it.
50	- Consistency: entries on the same subject agree, or state their different scopes or their conflict.
51	
52	An entry that fails scope, evidence or consistency is not kept as it stands: reword it to what its support holds, or investigate where the support is unresolved. A fail of comprehension or ownership asks for a rewrite. Give no score: good prose does not make up for an unsupported claim. Then give the entry one disposition:
53	
54	- keep: every check passes;
55	- reword: the meaning holds, but the wording or the stated scope fails;
56	- reorganize: move detail out, merge the entry into its owner, or split it;
57	- investigate: the support or the consistency is unresolved. Settle that narrow question before any new wording, and do not delete the fact meanwhile.
58	
59	Before you write or check the first entries of a consolidation, read the five worked examples: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/record-rule-draft.md#Worked examples'`, a large read.
60	
61	## Reading and writing
62	
63	- `git log -S'F-87' --oneline -- explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md` lists the commits that touched an entry.
64	- To read a history in depth, or a report's passage, send a Sonnet scout. The provenance lines tell it where to dig.
65	- `record.py`'s header gives its usage. `add`, `set`, `merge`, `remove` and `apply` write; each needs `--from PATH#HEADING` or `--note WHY`. The tool stamps the time and copies the earlier line to the history.
66	- Before every commit, run `record.py check --base <the commit before your edits>`. It shows that nothing was lost, and reports each entry over 600 characters.
67	- Commit the record file and its history together.
68	- Write a decision into POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it. A proposal of yours enters only at the curator's yes.
69	- The record is public and names models on purpose. Hold nothing back from it for that.
70	
71	## The pass
72	
73	Run the pass when a worker finishes, and before the next boot or batch reads FACTS. In a batch, the commit stage runs it, with this part quoted in its prompt. After a lone worker, you run it.
74	
75	The pass owns each entry's final wording. A rung writes its findings as draft entries: the claim, its conditions, its evidence and what it means.
76	
77	1. Write each new fact as an entry, or rewrite in place the entry that it changes. A rung writes its entries in a file `record.md` in its worktree, and the gather folds them in with `record.py apply`.
78	2. Give each change its provenance: the report section, the commit, and why.
79	3. Check each entry against its source, with bounded `grep`s:
80	   - The cited report section holds what the entry left out.
81	   - The entry keeps the source's scope: the path (walk or the compiled path), the call form (a dotted method call against a top-level call), the range of values and the conditions. Ask: does the entry let a reader conclude more than the evidence shows?
82	   - If a behaviour changed, grep FACTS for it, linked or not. Each entry that states it is updated, or says how it differs.
83	4. Cut any plan or status from each entry (above). If the cut text named a PLAN item or a review-queue item, check that the item names the entry.
84	5. Report each entry over 600 characters, with the question that keeps its extra sentence.
85	
86	Run the same pass on POSITIONS at each landing, and when the curator replaces a decision.
87	
88	## A consolidation
89	
90	A consolidation runs the pass over whole sections. After a batch lands, the record-landing workflow consolidates its entries (`references/batch.md`, "The landing").
91	
92	- In a consolidation, by hand or by the clarity or mining workflow, run a pilot of three or four entries first. Show their new texts to the curator as a page, each with its old text (`SKILL.md`, "Pages"). Run the rest on the curator's go. The pilot shows the curator the form: the length, the register, and what belongs in the history. The other checks, the pass's step 3, the tools' cold readers and the quiz, test only the meaning. The record-landing workflow takes no pilot, since it lands with no step of yours.
93	- Split each section into chunks of 20 to 32 entries.
94	- For each chunk, a Sonnet scout gathers each entry's report sections, its commits and the curator's dated words.
95	- An Opus writer reads this part, the chunk and the scout's file, and writes an apply file. It runs `apply` and `check --base` in its own worktree.
96	- You apply each file on `main`, run `check --base`, commit and push.
97	- Have Opus workers check each new entry by the pass's step 3. Run no Fable review of the entries.
98	- Have a fresh Opus worker answer a small quiz of decisions from the new entries, on the records at hand, without the curator. The decisions must stay as good, and the worker must follow the pointers when needed. If something critical is lost, find the middle ground entry by entry.
99	
100	## The consolidation tools
101	
102	Four Workflow scripts keep the record and the worker skill current and readable. Each one's README says how to run it and what to do with its output. Give a run only its arguments and the input files that its README names. Add no rules of your own over the tool's briefs, and change the briefs only where its README says to, such as their paths. If the briefs do not fit the job, propose their change to the curator. Put the open questions of the runs on the review queue.
103	
104	Pick the tool by the job:
105

- Split the items into chunks of about ten, or of the size that the workflow's README gives.
- Share the chunks evenly among the runs. Pass each run its share in its `chunks` argument.

- The script resumes a stream while its context is small and its prompt cache is warm. Its header gives the limits. Otherwise it starts a fresh session.
- So the round that fixes a chunk after its checks resumes the session that wrote it, with its evidence still in the cache. A fresh writer would read everything again.
- End each round with one judge. For each item that a chunk's checks raise, it rules apply or hold, and writes the held items for the review queue. No chunk goes through a second fix round.
- Only you write the record files, so the runs do not conflict.
- As each run ends, apply its judged chunks to the record, check the record, commit and push, by "After a chunk" in the workflow's README. Then take the next run that has ended.
- If a chunk splits or merges an entry that another chunk also changes, apply that chunk first.
- If an interrupt or a process stop kills the runs, resume each one from its ID in `runs.json`, as "Interrupts and process stops" says.

A file's skill is the folder after "skills/" in its path, so a copy made with
`git show REV:.claude/skills/...` into a folder of the same layout is linted
as the file it copies. A skill not named above takes every set.

With no FILE, every file under the repository's .claude/skills/. Prints
`path:line: set: text` for each hit, the text clipped around the match, and
exits 1 if there is any. Patterns are case-insensitive unless they say (?-i:...).

2	
3	# Writing the skills
4	
5	The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.
6	
7	## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else
8	
9	A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
10	- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
11	- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."
12	
13	## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them
14	
15	A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
16	- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
17	- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."
18	
19	## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest
20	
21	Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
22	- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
23	- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"
24	
25	## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work
26	
27	A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
28	- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
29	- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."
30	
31	Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.
32	
33	## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name
34	
35	A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
36	- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
37	- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."
38	
39	## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace
40	
41	The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
42	- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
43	- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."
44	
45	Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.
46	
47	## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read
48	
49	A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.

51	- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

# Cold read of the drafts B1 to B4, coordinator skill

Read as the coordinating session. For each draft I read the part around it on `main`, put the new text in place, and judged the result. Line numbers are those of the passage on `main` that the draft replaces. "Bn.m" names the draft.

## 1. The lint

Skipped, as the task says. One extra run, on the drafts' new texts alone, copied into a scratch folder laid out as `.claude/skills/coordinator/` (so the coordinator's sets apply): no hit, exit 0. One proposed fix below would add a hit if written as "way 2"; flag 26 says how to avoid it.

## 2. What I would do differently, section by section

- B1.1, "review queue": I would file in the queue only a consequential decision that waits for the curator's word. I could not tell where an objection, a workflow's held item or a run's open question goes (flag 2).
- B1.2, "default": I would treat a landed default as closed: FACTS states it, the landing report gives it. No queue item unless it is consequential.
- B1.3, "landing report": I would send one report after each batch landing, and look up its form in `batch.md`, "The landing", step 2.
- B1.4, "review list" deleted: I would keep no list "listed for his review" in PLAN.
- B1.5: I would decide a settled fork that is not consequential, and file it in no list.
- B1.6, the three ways: for a consequential decision that can be undone: land its default, name it in the landing report, keep its question in the queue with the work that needs the answer, and ask before that work starts. For every other decision: close it at its landing, state it in FACTS, give it in the landing report. Open a queue item only if the curator objects to its line.
- B1.7: I would put a queue item whose default landed as a decision already taken, never as a hold. No change in action.
- B1.8: I would tell the curator of no record edit except through the landing report and the POSITIONS report.
- B1.9: No change in action, only the list's name.
- B1.10: PLAN's line names no review lists. No change in action by itself.
- B1.11: Every landed worker choice gets a FACTS entry that says a worker chose it. Only a consequential one gets a queue item.
- B1.12: Overnight, I would take a consequential batch-record question's default, launch, and leave its question in the queue.
- B1.13: A settled fix at a reserved point or an unnamed file still lands. I would mention the point or the file in the landing report.
- B1.14: I would list the gate's hidden differences and rewritten test lines in "the batch's `RECORD.md`", but I would have to search for that file and for who writes it.
- B1.15: A reversible reserved point goes in the landing report. The merged-diff review's leftover findings go to "the post-batch review's list for the batch after", which I would have to search for.
- B1.16: I would send one message of at most about ten lines, each a behaviour change with its FACTS number, then a count and a link. I would open a queue item only on the curator's objection.
- B2.1: I would treat only rule changes of `fortress-repo` as needing the curator's notice.
- B2.2: On the `fortress-repo` page, only a rule change gets an item.
- B2.3: The page worker gives a rule change an item and every other change a foot line, and removes both at the second landing after.
